S01: Welcome. Today we will follow one **learning path** and see how AI can help. Our main question is simple: how can we use these tools while keeping **independent thinking** at the centre?
S02: I am Marco Cremaschi, an assistant professor at the University of Milano-Bicocca. My work connects **AI** with practical problems. I also teach visual communication, interface design and programming, including the use of technology in psychology and psychiatry.
S44: I also helped start **Whattadata**, a university spin-off. We use data and AI to solve practical problems, with attention to people and the limits of the technology. This work connects my research with real applications.
S48: Today we will bring these ideas into **classroom practice**. We will use learning maps and short activities to explore goals, feedback and self-assessment. The aim is to give you ideas you can adapt to your own students.
S50: For teachers, the aim is to build an **activity you can reuse** in your subject. We will connect a clear goal with a visual task and a check of understanding. You can use the prepared materials or your own examples.
S50QR: Before we begin, scan the **QR code** to open the EduForum slides. I will give you a moment. You can use the links to follow the examples and return to them later.
S50LEGEND: As you follow the slides, these **icons** show who each activity is for: teachers, students, or both. They will help you find the examples most useful to you.
S51: Let us make this concrete with **Andrea**, a computer science student. He can program, but he still confuses some ideas about generative AI. He needs to study a chapter and explain how a language model produces text. We will follow his learning process; **you do not need programming knowledge**.
S52:
Andrea needs to understand the chapter and show what he has learned. We will follow **four connected activities**.

[click] First, he **reads** the chapter and notes what is unclear.

[click] Then, he **represents** the ideas in a diagram and explains the links.

[click] Next, he **checks** the diagram and AI suggestions against the chapter, correcting any errors.

[click] Finally, he **explains** a new example in his own words, without AI. His diagram, explanation and corrections show us what he understands.
S52SDL: These activities ask Andrea to make his own learning choices. This is **self-directed learning**: he sets a goal, chooses how to study and reviews his progress. **Teachers and peers** can help, while he remains responsible for his choices.
S52SA: But how does Andrea know if his choices are working? Through **self-assessment**: he checks his work against clear criteria. For example, he can explain the ideas but struggles with the links, so he revises his map. AI can offer feedback, but **Andrea decides what needs more work**.
S53: To try this, Andrea needs a **great book**, by a great author. I am joking, of course. This is a **fictional book** made for the workshop, with real explanations and technical references. We will use its chapter to check AI answers and Andrea's understanding.
S53WHYTOOLS:
With the chapter ready, why choose these tools? **ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude** are alternatives; you can choose one. **NotebookLM** adds a workspace for selected sources. You do not need paid access to all of them. There are four reasons for this choice.

[click] First, they give us **more control**. We can ask for a simpler explanation or one question at a time, based on our goal.

[click] Second, we can **connect our study tasks**. We can use the same chapter for explanations, diagrams and practice, checking each result.

[click] Third, we practise **skills we can reuse**. Setting goals and checking answers help us in other subjects too.

[click] Finally, we may **save money**. One assistant may cover several needs, although free access has limits. We can add a specialist tool when it helps. Let us start with ChatGPT.
S53GPT: With **ChatGPT**, we start from Andrea's need. Does he need to understand an idea, build a map or practise an answer? The tool can prepare material, but Andrea still needs to **explain or revise it himself**. Let us see how to ask.
S53SHORTCUTS: One quick way to ask is to use a **shortcut**. Some shortcuts are features in the app. Others are simply words we put in a prompt to describe the task. Let us look at the difference.
S53TYPES:
We can ask for help in **two ways**: choose an app feature or write a request.

[click] A **formal action**, such as Study, is a feature we select in the app.

[click] The second way is to **describe an activity**. For example: “/quiz: use this chapter to ask me one question at a time and give feedback on my answers.” Here, **/quiz** is a short label; the rest tells the AI what to do. We can also describe any buttons we want.
S53FORMALWEB: Here is the first type in practice. Andrea selects **Study** and asks for one question at a time, based on the chapter. A wrong answer leads to a hint and another attempt. Afterwards, he still needs to **explain the idea without AI** and check it against the source.
S53FORMALREADALOUD: Another built-in feature is **Read aloud**. It reads a ChatGPT response so Andrea can listen to the explanation again. It is available outside Study too. Listening gives him another way to review, but he still needs to check what he understands.
S53SHORTCUTCLOUD: Now let us explore the **15 prompt examples**. Each one supports a learning action, such as recall, explanation or planning. You can select a label to see its purpose and open the recording. As we look, think about which activity would help Andrea with his current difficulty.
S53CMD1: The first group helps Andrea **recall and review**. With /flashcard, he answers before revealing the explanation. With /mistakelog, he keeps track of errors and corrections. Together, they help him choose what to study again.
S53CMD2: Once he knows the terms, Andrea needs to **connect the ideas**. He can build a concept map, match definitions or sort examples. Oral practice then asks him to explain those links in his own words. For each activity, he checks his reasoning against the chapter.
S53CMD3: Next, Andrea can **test his understanding**. A quiz or missing-word task checks specific points. A worksheet asks for a written explanation, while a case study uses a new example. In each case, he answers first, then reads the feedback and explains any correction.
S53CMD4: These activities also need a **plan**. Andrea can use /studyplan to choose his next steps. Teachers can plan a lesson, adjust the level of support or set up learning stations. Shared criteria can guide peer feedback. Let us now see the examples in more detail.
S53DETAILQUIZ: A **quiz** gives him another quick check. Andrea chooses an answer before reading the feedback. If he makes a mistake, he uses the explanation to revise. The useful question is: why is the corrected answer right?
S53DETAILMATCHINGGAME: If the terms are still unclear, Andrea can start with **matching**. Here he pairs concepts with definitions. After each match, he explains the link in a sentence. A correct pair is a useful start; his explanation shows whether he understands it.
S53DETAILFILLINTHEBLANKS: To check the terms in a sentence, Andrea can try **fill in the blanks**. He enters the missing words, checks them and corrects any errors. He then explains the whole sentence, including why each word fits.
S53DETAILFLASHCARD: We begin with **flashcards** made from the chapter. Andrea answers from memory, reveals the explanation and rates his recall. That rating moves him to the next card. He can download the ten questions and answers as a **CSV file** for later review.
S53DETAILSORTINGGAME: Next, he uses those meanings to **sort examples** into training or inference. The key question stays the same: do the model's parameters change, or does it use information to produce a response? The feedback helps Andrea check and explain his choice.
S53DETAILORAL: Andrea also needs to prepare for an **oral exam**. Here he can type or dictate an answer, then reveal the expected explanation. He compares it with his own words and the chapter. He can return to earlier questions and improve his answers.
S53DETAILSTUDYPLAN: His answers help Andrea decide **what to study next**. This plan breaks his goal into smaller activities. He can mark his progress and move between steps. After each activity, he checks what he can explain or do on his own.
S53DETAILCONCEPTMAP: Some errors concern the links between ideas. This **concept map** connects training, inference and RAG. The key questions are: when do parameters change, and when is information added to the context? Andrea explains each link, checks the chapter and corrects his answer if needed.
S53DETAILMISTAKELOG: When a card reveals an error, Andrea can add it to a **mistake log**. He writes the correction and explains why his first answer was wrong. He can then mark the item as understood or keep it for another review.
S53DETAILLESSONPLAN: For teachers, the same approach becomes a **15-minute lesson**: four minutes to explain, six to apply and five to assess. Students compare fine-tuning, a prompt definition and a retrieved passage. They explain what changes before seeing the answer, then finish with an explanation on their own.
S53DETAILCASESTUDY: Now Andrea can apply these ideas to a **case study**. He compares training a model, changing a prompt and adding retrieved material. He writes his answer before revealing the explanation. In each case, what changes: the parameters or the context?
S53DETAILDIFFERENTIATE: Students may need different levels of help. These **three levels** keep the same learning goal but change the support and difficulty. We start from the learner's needs, then reduce the clues. A new example checks whether the learner can explain the idea independently.
S53DETAILPEERASSESSMENT: Students can also help each other check their work. **Peer assessment** starts with shared criteria. Here, a fictional peer gives points and written feedback. The feedback names one strength and one thing to improve, with evidence from the answer.
S53DETAILWORKSHEET: For a longer answer, we can use a **worksheet**. Andrea writes his explanation before revealing a model answer. He compares the work with the criteria and gives himself points. The score is a summary; his written answer shows what he understands.
S53DETAILLEARNINGSTATIONS: We can bring several activities together in **learning stations**. Each station focuses on training, inference or context. Andrea writes an answer, compares it with the explanation and marks the station complete. He can return to earlier answers and revise them.
S53TRYSHORTCUTS: Now it is **your turn**. Take ten minutes to try /flashcard, /quiz or /oral in your ChatGPT account. The Free plan is fine. Use our chapter or your own document. Try the activity, check its answers against your source and adjust the request if needed.
S53SKILLSSECTION: We have used separate prompts for individual tasks. What if we want to reuse a whole method? This is where **Agent Skills** can help. Let us look at how they guide a task from start to finish.
S53SKILLS: A **skill** is a set of instructions an agent can reuse for a task. Its main file, **SKILL.md**, explains when to use it and what steps to follow. It may also include examples, templates or scripts. The agent loads these files when it needs them.
S53SKILLHOSTS: Before using a skill, we need to check **where it can run**. These examples were recorded in ChatGPT Work mode. Other agents may support skills but provide different tools. We need to check the setup as well as the skill itself.
S53SKILLSTUDY:
Here are **three skills** for the same chapter. The first, **Learn**, uses questions and feedback to help Andrea understand.

[click] **The Learning Skill** adds study materials, practice and review.

[click] Finally, **Markdown Mermaid Writing** creates diagrams we can edit. The chapter stays the same; we choose the skill for Andrea's next need and check the result.
S53SKILLLEARN: Let us start with **Learn**. Andrea thinks a definition in a prompt changes the model's weights. The skill asks him to explain, then uses the chapter to correct the idea: prompts change context; training changes parameters. A question about RAG checks whether he can use this distinction again.
S53SKILLLEARNING: Next, **The Learning Skill** builds a kit after Andrea tries to recall the ideas. It plans ten minutes today and two five-minute reviews. He retries a card and checks a written answer. The shared chat shows the code; the **HTML download** gives us the interactive kit.
S53SKILLMERMAID: For links between ideas, we can use an **editable diagram**. This example separates training, inference and retrieval. Andrea checks each arrow against the chapter. He then closes the diagram and explains the relationship in his own words.
S53TOOLSSECTION: Skills give us a method we can reuse. Now let us look at **specific study tools**. We will keep asking two questions: what problem does this tool help with, and how will Andrea show what he has learned?
S58TOOLGOBLIN: Andrea's first problem may be **getting started**. Goblin.tools can help him turn a large task into smaller actions. Let us see how he can use its suggestions to build a plan that fits his goal.
S58COMPILER: First, **Compiler** turns Andrea's rough thoughts into suggested actions. Here it gives him four tasks. He checks that they match his learning goal and the time he has. The suggestions give him a starting point; he chooses what to keep.
S58: A task can still be too large to start. **Magic ToDo** breaks it into smaller steps that Andrea can edit. He adds enough detail to know what to do next. He does not need a separate step for every small action.
S58ESTIMATOR: With the steps ready, Andrea needs to plan his **time**. Estimator suggests a rough time window. He compares it with how long the task actually takes, then adjusts his plan. The estimate helps him plan; it is not a promise.
S58TASKMASTER: Now he is ready to begin. **Taskmaster** focuses on one task and shows a timer. The timer tells Andrea how long he has worked. To check his learning, he still needs to look at what he can explain or produce.
S58PROFESSOR: While working, Andrea may get stuck on an idea. **Professor** offers an explanation and an example of training and inference. He checks both against the chapter. If it uses an analogy, he also checks where that comparison stops being useful.
S58FORMALIZER: Once Andrea has an explanation, **Formalizer** can help make the wording clearer. He compares the rewrite with his draft. Does it keep the same meaning? Does it still show what he is unsure about? Clearer writing should preserve those details.
S59: These examples bring us back to one rule: make the **next action clear**. Reading one paragraph and writing an example is easier to start than a broad goal. Add detail when it helps Andrea move past a real difficulty.
S60: Andrea now chooses his own plan: **read, ask, reconstruct and apply**. He notes unclear ideas, checks an explanation, rebuilds the diagram and tries a new example. Each step leaves something he can check. Finished tasks show activity; the work itself shows what he understands.
S61TOOLNOTEBOOK: With a plan ready, Andrea needs a place to **study his sources**. NotebookLM lets him ask questions and create materials from selected documents. We will use it with his chapter and keep checking answers against the original text.
S61: We begin by **adding the chapter**. Andrea checks the imported text and selects the sources for his question. This keeps the task focused, but the answer can still contain errors. He will need to check it against the chapter.
S61RESEARCH: If the chapter is not enough, Andrea can **search for more sources**. Before importing a result, he checks who produced it, whether it answers his question and whether it is reliable. Finding a source does not mean he should use it.
S61DEEP: For a wider question, **Deep Research** can prepare a report with sources. Andrea still needs to read those sources and check the claims. This feature requires an adult account, so we also need to check access before planning an activity.
S62: Let us return to Andrea's main question: **why can an answer change without retraining?** He asks a short, focused question. He then compares the explanation and its references with the chapter. This gives him a manageable answer to check.
S63: To check that answer, Andrea opens the **citation** and reads the passage. Here, the words **ordinary inference** matter: they describe when the model's parameters stay fixed. He checks that the passage supports the exact claim in the answer.
S64SETTINGS: We can also change how the conversation works. With **Learning Guide**, we choose a goal and a response length that leave room for Andrea to answer. The settings should support his own explanation and practice.
S65: An explanation may use an **analogy**, but we need to check that too. The desk example helps explain available context. It does not explain how a model calculates. Andrea should be able to explain the idea without relying on the comparison.
S66: This is the map created with **Mind Map**. It connects training, inference, context and RAG. We can zoom in to read each branch. Where do parameters change, and where is information added as input? Andrea checks the links against the chapter, then explains them without the map.
S67: These six questions were created with **Quiz**. Let us try one before showing the answer. We can choose an option, ask for a hint and read the explanation. Andrea then explains any correction in his own words. This viewer uses the original generated questions and feedback.
S67CARDS: These cards were created with **Flashcards**. Let us answer the first question from memory, then show the answer. We can move through the cards and compare each explanation with the chapter. The viewer uses the exported questions and answers; the CSV is also available to download.
S67NOTES: When Andrea finds a useful explanation, he can **save it as a note**. The note keeps the response and its citations, including any errors. He checks it before using it again or turning it into a new source.
S67REPORTS: This study guide was created with **Reports**. We can turn the pages and zoom in to read it. Andrea checks its definitions and examples against the chapter. He then uses the guide to prepare questions and explain the ideas himself.
S67AUDIO: This episode was created with **Audio Overview**. Let us listen to a short part, then pause. How would you explain that idea in your own words? Andrea can use the same approach when studying, checking his explanation against the chapter before he continues.
S67VIDEO: This is the video created with **Video Overview**, with its original English audio. It compares training, inference and RAG. Let us pause after an example and check it against the chapter. Andrea then explains the difference himself.
S67INFO: This image was created with **Infographic**. It compares training, inference and RAG in one view. We can zoom in to read the details. Andrea checks the labels against the chapter, then explains what changes in each process.
S67SLIDES: These nine slides were created with **Slide Deck**. We can move through the PDF to compare training, inference and RAG. What changes in each case? Andrea checks the labels and arrows against the chapter, then answers the final question without the slides.
S67TABLES: This comparison was created with **Data Table**. It shows what changes and what stays fixed in training, inference and RAG. We can show the extra columns to check the chapter evidence and common errors. Those errors are claims to reject, not facts to learn.

We provide the checked answer as a text download instead. For your own class, test access as a student before the session.
S97: To help you choose tools after today, these tables group them by purpose. We start with **free tools**. Choose the function you need, then check the access conditions. Some free plans still need an account or have limits, so keep a prepared alternative.
S97STUDY: For maps and review, we have more focused options. **Drawing tools** help us explain relationships; **review tools** help us return to questions over time. Choose the action that fits the learning need. We can keep using the same source and checks.
S97P: Some tools offer more features through a **paid plan**. Before paying, compare the feature you need with a free option and check the current terms. A paid tool is useful only if the extra feature helps with your task.

S52PHASES:
We can organise Andrea's study into **six phases**. Each phase helps him choose what to do next.

[click] First, he **plans** a goal and his study time.

[click] To **understand** an idea, he works through an explanation or example.

[click] He then **connects** it with what he already knows, using a map.

[click] Next, he tries to **recall** it without the chapter, and reviews it again later.

[click] To **apply** it, he tries a new example.

[click] Finally, he **checks** his answer against the source and criteria. He can return to an earlier phase when needed. The ribbon shows the main and secondary phases. **Support** covers setup, sources and sharing.
S97ACCESS: We also need to consider **accessibility**. Reading aloud and dictation can support different stages of learning. Choose the support with the learner. Check the languages available and review dictated text. Read&Write offers a wider set of tools through a licence.

S53GEMINI:
The **Gemini** tests gave mixed results. Each prompt used the same chapter in a new chat. Of the 15 prompts, two gave interactive activities directly in Gemini, five gave working apps to download, four gave material without interactive controls and four failed to generate a result.

For the downloaded apps, I asked Gemini to show the activity in Canvas. The previews stayed blank here, so I tested the downloaded files locally without changing them. Those screenshots are labelled **exported app**.

The same prompt can give a different result in another assistant. **Test the controls and check the content** before using it with students.
